analysis.one_liner: Makes oil spillers pay full cleanup and damage costs and requires double-hulled oil tankers.
analysis.headline: It passed the House 375-5 and the Senate 99-0, and the President signed it into law as Public Law 101-380 on August 18, 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the Exxon Valdez disaster, the law makes the company responsible for an oil spill pay for the cleanup and for damages to people whose property, jobs, or natural resources were hurt. It uses a federal trust fund so cleanup and claims get paid quickly, then bills the spiller back. It also requires double hulls for new oil tankers, stricter crew and pilot rules, mandatory spill-response plans, and much larger fines for companies that fail to report a spill.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishermen, tourism businesses, and state and local governments gain a guaranteed way to recover losses from an oil spill, including lost income, lost subsistence use of resources, and lost tax revenue. Taxpayers gain because the spiller, not the public, is the first line of payment for cleanups, and prevention rules lower the odds of a spill in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: It puts the cost of a spill on the spiller: the responsible party owes strict liability for all removal costs and for damages including property loss, lost income and earning capacity, loss of subsistence use of natural resources, and lost state and local tax revenue.

It channels money through the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund so cleanup and claims get paid quickly after a disaster, with up to $1 billion available per incident and states able to draw on the fund for their own response costs.

It aims to prevent the next disaster: new tankers must have double hulls, single-hulled tankers in Prince William Sound must take tug escorts and state-licensed pilots past Bligh Reef, crews face drug and alcohol testing, and operators must file and practice worst-case spill response plans.
It creates citizen oversight councils for Prince William Sound and Cook Inlet, funded by terminal and tanker operators, that monitor operations and must be consulted before federal permit decisions.

It raises the price of cutting corners: civil penalties rise to as much as $25,000 per day or $1,000 per barrel discharged, and failing to report a spill can now bring up to three years in prison instead of one.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, tanker owners, and offshore facility operators pay through strict liability for spills, mandatory financial-responsibility proof, double-hull construction and retrofit costs, higher penalties, and a per-barrel tax into the trust fund. Some of those costs are passed through to consumers in the price of fuel.

drawbacks.text: Damages owed by a spiller are capped (with specified exceptions), and the federal trust fund can pay no more than $1 billion per incident — in a truly catastrophic spill, some losses could go uncompensated once the caps are hit.
Double-hull requirements, liability insurance, and the per-barrel tax that feeds the trust fund raise the cost of moving oil, costs that are largely passed to consumers at the pump.

The final law carves the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System out of the act's general liability rules, substituting its own regime with a $350 million damages cap — special treatment for the pipeline consortium that its sponsors had to accept to close the deal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but deliberately placed on the industry whose tankers and pipelines create the risk, and only part of them reach consumers through fuel prices. The main concession to industry is the cap on damages and the Alaska pipeline carve-out, which honest supporters would concede could leave victims underpaid after a worst-case disaster; unlimited removal-cost liability, the fund, and the prevention mandates are the offsetting strengths. On balance the deal traded a modest industry subsidy (caps, pipeline carve-out) for a nationwide guarantee that spills get cleaned up and victims get paid.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by near-unanimous votes and the President signed it on August 18, 1990, making it Public Law 101-380.

narrative.text: The bill was written in the months after the Exxon Valdez ran aground in Prince William Sound: its text requires monitoring of the effects of the Exxon Valdez discharge and adds special protections for that Sound, including tug escorts, state-licensed pilots past Bligh Reef, and prepositioned cleanup equipment.
The House passed its version 375-5 on November 9, 1989, after weeks of floor amendments offered by members including George Miller of California.

The Senate took up the House bill, struck its text and substituted its own broader bill (S. 686, which added the double-hull mandate and a compensation fund), and passed it by voice vote on November 19, 1989.

On February 7, 1990, the House voted 376-37 to instruct its conferees to insist that new and existing tank vessels carry double bottoms or double hulls, signaling that the double-hull requirement had to survive the House-Senate negotiation.

The final conference report — which kept the double-hull mandate, the $1 billion-per-incident fund, and the liability regime — was approved by the Senate 99-0 on August 2, 1990 and by the House 360-0 on August 4, 1990, and was signed into law on August 18, 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishermen, and state governments came out ahead with a guaranteed cleanup-and-compensation system funded first by the spiller; the oil-shipping industry also came out ahead in one respect, trading liability caps, a $350 million pipeline carve-out, and a public backstop fund for acceptance of double hulls and stricter liability.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities and fishermen; industry got caps

sides.party_line_note: Support was near-unanimous across both parties: the Senate approved the final version 99-0 with all 54 Democrats and 45 Republicans voting yes, the House passed it 375-5 and later 360-0 with every voting member of both parties in favor.

industries.note: The law makes them strictly liable for cleanup and damages, requires proof of financial responsibility, mandates double hulls, and raises penalties and per-barrel taxes. Their gain — a single predictable federal liability regime replacing a patchwork of older funds — is outweighed by the new costs, and their interest in limiting liability ran against the public's interest in full compensation.

industries.industry: Oil spill response and cleanup industry
industries.note: Mandatory response plans, prepositioned equipment, periodic drills, regional strike teams, and a national equipment inventory create a standing market for spill-response services and equipment.
The double-hull construction mandate for tank vessels generates new building and retrofit work, and the law adds federal loan guarantees to help finance vessel construction.
These businesses can now recover lost income, profits, and earning capacity after a spill, and the Prince William Sound provisions directly protect the fishing grounds hurt by the Exxon Valdez.

The final law exempts the pipeline system from the act's general liability regime, but substitutes its own rules: strict liability for all removal costs and up to $350 million in damages, plus a $1,000-per-barrel spill penalty. The carve-out limits their exposure while still holding them to a strict standard.
